scene.metaphor: A miniature workshop conveyor turns a heap of raw chat snippets into neatly sorted labeled chips, like a hand-built quality-control line for language.
scene.setting: Polished studio photograph of a cool-gray tabletop workshop set, with a long lateral conveyor running across a wide 3:1 frame. The background fades to generous negative space in soft gray, while cobalt and mint tools punctuate the set. Tal stands at the left-third as the operator, facing the line.
scene.frozen_incident: At the exact moment a small pile of loose, paper-like conversation cards slides off a tilted feeder tray, Tal calmly catches the spill with one hand while his other hand keeps a mint sorting gate aligned, as if this is a normal part of the job.
physical_materials: hand-cut paper cards with no readable text
one restrained warm accent in Tal’s coral tank top
semantic_anchors: raw language as unorganized physical cards
annotation as sorting into labeled stations
work as a sequence of distinct stages
gold standard as a tidy final bin
automation as a small assistive mechanism
quality control and review as manual hands-on checking
compounding improvement as an orderly line
avoid: humiliation or chaos beyond the harmless spill
scene.image_instruction: Create a polished studio editorial photograph of Tal Perry as a calm workshop operator in a miniature language-annotation assembly line. He should be clearly recognizable, smiling with focused, wry concentration, wearing his coral tank top as the only warm accent against a cool-gray, cobalt, and mint palette. Build a long, low set that reads laterally in a 3:1 banner: a conveyor of hand-cut blank chat cards moves from a messy intake pile on the left through three to five small practical stations into tidy bins on the right, suggesting raw data becoming dependable labeled material. Freeze a harmless incident at the center: one tray has tipped and a few cards are sliding, while Tal steadies the line with one hand and guides a mint sorting gate with the other. Use tactile materials—felt, acrylic, brushed metal, paper, wood—and strong tonal separation with one dominant subject, no more than three large supporting props, and generous negative space so the scene stays legible at thumbnail size.
